title: What Dataflow Gen2 actually is
prompt: A teammate describes Dataflow Gen2 as "a semantic model that refreshes lookup tables". Which correction states what it really is?

options.text: A cloud-hosted Power Query pipeline: reusable, refreshable ingestion and transformation queries that land data in storage destinations of your choice.
options.why: Correct. Gen2 is the Power Query experience in Fabric, storing its results in destinations rather than only inside a model.

options.text: A scheduled backup of lakehouse tables.
options.why: It is neither a backup nor tied to lakehouse tables alone.

options.text: A semantic-model partition type.
options.why: Semantic models can read from dataflows, but the dataflow itself is not a partition.

options.text: A Spark notebook wrapper.
options.why: Notebooks are a different engine; the decision guide treats them as separate tools.

explanation: Dataflow Gen2 brings Power Query authoring into Fabric as a first-class, refreshable item with its own data destinations.

title: Copy, dataflow, or notebook
prompt: A source CSV needs three joins, six derived columns, and a type-conversion chain before landing in a lakehouse table, and the analyst maintaining it is a Power Query expert. Which tool matches?

options.text: A Dataflow Gen2 authored in Power Query.
options.why: Correct. The decision guide positions dataflows for reusable Power Query transformations; copy tools do not express rich multi-step logic.

options.text: A Copy activity with field mappings.
options.why: Copy moves data with light mappings; three joins and a transformation chain exceed its job.

options.text: A Spark notebook, because Spark is always the better transform engine.
options.why: The guide picks by skill fit and transformation shape, not by engine prestige.

options.text: A KQL materialized view.
options.why: Wrong engine entirely: the source is CSV and the logic is relational shaping.

explanation: The documented decision guide orders the tools by what the work actually is: movement (Copy), Power Query transformation (dataflow), or custom code (notebook).

title: Where a dataflow can land
prompt: Which set of destinations is documented for Dataflow Gen2 data output?

options.text: Fabric Lakehouse tables.
options.why: Correct — a documented data destination.

options.text: Fabric Warehouse tables.
options.why: Correct — a documented data destination.

options.text: Azure SQL Database tables.
options.why: Correct — a documented data destination, including Azure SQL in the list.

options.text: A Power BI report canvas.
options.why: Incorrect — reports consume models; they are not a data destination.

explanation: The documented data destinations include lakehouse and warehouse tables plus Azure SQL Database (and other stores); a report is a consumer, never a landing zone.

title: One query, two lands
prompt: A cleaned customer query must land both in a lakehouse table for analysts and in a Warehouse table for finance. What does Dataflow Gen2 support?

options.text: Multiple data destinations per query — the same query's output can be written to more than one destination.
options.why: Correct. A query can declare several data destinations; the documented destination experience allows multiple outputs per query.

options.text: One destination per dataflow, so two dataflows must duplicate the logic.
options.why: That is Gen1-era thinking; Gen2 destinations are per-query and multiple are supported.

options.text: One destination per refresh, alternated by parameter.
options.why: There is no per-refresh destination switching.

options.text: Only one destination type per dataflow (mixing lakehouse and warehouse is unsupported).
options.why: Mixing destination types across queries is supported.

explanation: Data destinations attach to queries; the documented experience supports multiple destinations, which is exactly how a single cleaned entity can serve two consumers.

title: Why queries stage
prompt: In the dataflow editor, most intermediate queries show a "staging" toggle enabled. What does staging do?

options.text: It lands intermediate query results into a staging area so later queries compute against stored intermediates instead of re-evaluating the whole chain.
options.why: Correct. Staging stores intermediate results, letting downstream queries and destinations read prepared data rather than recomputing.

options.text: It versions the query definition for source control.
options.why: Draft/save and Git handle versioning; staging is about data.

options.text: It caches credentials for the source.
options.why: Credential caching is unrelated to the staging toggle.

options.text: It schedules the query for off-peak refresh.
options.why: Scheduling belongs to the dataflow's refresh settings, not to staging.

explanation: Staging is the documented performance mechanism: intermediate queries persist their results, and the destinations compute from prepared intermediates.

title: Landing directly, no staging
prompt: A simple pass-through query copies one source table straight into a lakehouse table. The team wonders whether staging helps here. What is the documented guidance?

options.text: For simple pass-through loads, disabling staging lets the data land directly in the destination without an intermediate store.
options.why: Correct. Staging earns its cost on complex graphs; a straight copy can skip it and land directly.

options.text: Staging must always remain enabled for lakehouse destinations.
options.why: It is a per-query choice, and simple loads are exactly where turning it off is suggested.

options.text: Disabling staging disables scheduled refresh.
options.why: Refresh scheduling is independent of staging.

options.text: Staging improves compression of the final destination table.
options.why: Staging stores intermediates; it does not compress the destination.

explanation: The documented managed-settings guidance: staging is a tool for complex graphs, and pass-through queries are the case where landing directly is cheaper.

title: Independent of the model
prompt: Finance's semantic model reads from a dataflow's lakehouse output. The dataflow refreshes at 06:00; the model refreshes at 06:30. What does this decoupling give the team?

options.text: The transformation work runs once in the dataflow; the model refresh ingests already-processed data — failures in one do not force the other's transformation to rerun.
options.why: Correct. Gen2 stores its output in the destination, so model refreshes consume prepared tables instead of re-running Power Query.

options.text: The model refresh re-executes the Power Query chain each time.
options.why: That is the Gen1 coupling; Gen2's destinations break it.

options.text: The dataflow cannot be scheduled separately from the model.
options.why: Dataflows have their own scheduled refresh.

options.text: The lakehouse table is rewritten by the model refresh.
options.why: The model reads the table; it does not rewrite it.

explanation: Gen2's defining architectural change is storage outside the model: transformation cost is paid in the dataflow, and consumers refresh against stored results.

title: Reading the refresh history
prompt: A dataflow refresh failed at 06:02. Where does the documented monitoring surface show the failure and its per-query detail?

options.text: The dataflow's refresh history / monitoring view, which lists refresh runs with start/end times and status.
options.why: Correct. The documented monitoring experience lists refresh runs and their outcomes for the dataflow.

options.text: The Real-Time hub.
options.why: The hub catalogs streams; refresh runs are not its subject.

options.text: The lakehouse's SQL endpoint query history.
options.why: That shows queries against the endpoint, not dataflow refreshes.

options.text: The deployment pipeline's compare view.
options.why: Pipeline compare diffs releases, not refresh runs.

explanation: Dataflow monitoring documents refresh runs with statuses and timing — the first stop when a scheduled refresh fails.

title: The on-premises SQL Server
prompt: One source is an on-premises SQL Server reachable only through the corporate network. How does a Dataflow Gen2 connect?

options.text: Through the on-premises data gateway, which the cloud service uses to reach the source.
options.why: Correct. On-premises sources are reached via the data gateway, as documented for dataflows.

options.text: Dataflows are cloud-only and cannot reach on-premises sources at all.
options.why: Gateway support is documented for dataflows.

options.text: By mirroring the SQL Server into Fabric first.
options.why: Mirroring is a different (and for on-prem SQL Server, not the applicable) replication feature.

options.text: By exposing the server on the public internet.
options.why: That is the security anti-pattern the gateway exists to avoid.

explanation: The on-premises data gateway is the documented bridge for cloud services reaching private sources, dataflows included.

title: The Dataflow activity
prompt: A pipeline must run three dataflows in order, then a notebook. Which pipeline activity runs a Dataflow Gen2 as a step?

options.text: The Dataflow activity, which invokes a dataflow's refresh as a pipeline step with its own success/failure semantics.
options.why: Correct. The documented Dataflow activity runs a dataflow inside a pipeline.

options.text: A Copy activity pointed at the dataflow item.
options.why: Copy moves data between stores; it cannot run a dataflow.

options.text: A Notebook activity with a %run of the dataflow.
options.why: Notebooks cannot execute dataflows; the Dataflow activity exists for this.

options.text: A Web activity calling the Power BI REST API.
options.why: An API path exists in principle, but the documented, native orchestration is the Dataflow activity.

explanation: The Dataflow activity is the documented orchestration primitive: dataflows become pipeline steps with dependencies, retries and alerts like any other activity.

title: Incremental through the tutorial pattern
prompt: The team wants a large source ingested incrementally, using Dataflow Gen2 orchestrated by a pipeline. Which documented tutorial pattern matches this goal?

options.text: Setup incremental refresh with Dataflows Gen2: pipeline-driven runs that filter source data by a changing boundary so each run moves only new data.
options.why: Correct. The documented tutorial demonstrates exactly this orchestration-driven incremental pattern.

options.text: Semantic-model incremental refresh policies applied to the dataflow.
options.why: Those policies govern model partitions, not dataflow runs.

options.text: Mirroring the source into the lakehouse.
options.why: Mirroring is replication for supported sources, not the dataflow pattern the question asks for.

options.text: A materialized view over the destination table.
options.why: Views accelerate queries; they do not filter what the next ingest moves.

explanation: The documented Gen2 incremental pattern couples the dataflow with pipeline orchestration and a moving boundary so each run transfers only new data.

title: Source control for the flow
prompt: The platform team wants dataflow definitions in Git and promoted through deployment pipelines like the rest of the estate. What is the documented state of support?

options.text: Dataflow Gen2 has documented CI/CD support: Git integration plus deployment pipelines, including connection and parameter concerns between stages.
options.why: Correct. The dedicated CI/CD page documents Git and pipeline support for Gen2.

options.text: Only Gen1 dataflows support Git; Gen2 definitions cannot leave the workspace.
options.why: The documented support is for Gen2.

options.text: Git support exists, but deployment pipelines reject dataflow items.
options.why: Deployment pipelines accept dataflow items per the documented CI/CD page.

options.text: Definitions export only as .pbix files.
options.why: That is not the dataflow CI/CD mechanism.

explanation: Dataflow Gen2 ships with documented CI/CD: the definition travels through Git and deployment pipelines, with stage configuration to review (connections, parameters).

title: Gen1 to Gen2
prompt: An old workspace still runs Dataflow Gen1. Which documented migration aids exist for moving it to Gen2?

options.text: A Save-as / migrate path that creates a Gen2 dataflow from an existing Gen1 dataflow.
options.why: Correct — the documented migration route.

options.text: An export-template feature for moving definitions.
options.why: Correct — the documented template export aids the move.

options.text: Gen1 dataflows are automatically converted in place on a fixed date.
options.why: Incorrect — migration is a documented manual aid, not an automatic conversion.

options.text: A dedicated REST endpoint that rewrites Gen1 mashup code into Spark.
options.why: Incorrect — no such automatic rewrite exists in the documented guidance.

explanation: The documented migration story is assisted, not automatic: save-as conversion and template export move definitions, with a documented guidance page for the differences.

title: Drafts before publish
prompt: An analyst wants to build a long transformation graph across two working sessions without refreshing anything yet. Which documented capability fits?

options.text: Saving the dataflow as a draft, keeping the in-progress queries without publishing or refreshing them.
options.why: Correct. The documented draft feature keeps unfinished work out of the refresh path.

options.text: Publishing immediately and disabling all queries.
options.why: Publishing to then neuter queries is not the draft mechanism.

options.text: Authoring in Notepad and pasting later.
options.why: There is no documented need to leave the tool; drafts exist.

options.text: Cloning the entire workspace as a backup.
options.why: Workspace cloning is heavyweight and not the authoring-time feature.

explanation: The documented draft capability is the authoring-time answer: keep the graph, skip the publish/refresh until it is ready.

title: What folds and what does not
prompt: A query filters a SQL source, then adds a custom column calling a local Python-free M function, then sorts. Which statement about query folding for the SQL source is accurate?

options.text: The source filter and sort can fold to the source; steps that cannot be translated (like the custom M function) create a local evaluation boundary after the last folded step.
options.why: Correct. Folding stops where M cannot be translated; everything after runs locally, which is why step order matters.

options.text: Dataflow Gen2 never folds; all data always arrives locally first.
options.why: Folding to capable sources is a documented Power Query behavior.

options.text: Adding any step always disables folding for the entire query.
options.why: Folding is per-step-prefix, not all-or-nothing for the query.

options.text: Sorting always prevents folding because it is client-side only.
options.why: Sorts translate to ORDER BY on capable sources.

explanation: Power Query folds what the source can execute and evaluates the rest locally; the custom function marks the boundary — a core reason to keep translatable steps early.

title: Reading the benchmarks
prompt: Before a large migration, the team wants documented expectations for Gen2 refresh cost and performance behavior. Which resource fits?

options.text: The published Dataflow Gen2 cost and performance benchmarks page.
options.why: Correct. A dedicated benchmarks page documents measured cost/performance behavior for Gen2 refreshes.

options.text: The Copilot get-started page.
options.why: Copilot onboarding is not a benchmarks source.

options.text: The Real-Time hub catalog.
options.why: Unrelated to dataflow performance.

options.text: The Power BI REST API reference.
options.why: API references list endpoints, not performance measurements.

explanation: A documented benchmarks page exists precisely so sizing conversations start from measurements rather than folklore.

title: Assisted authoring
prompt: A junior analyst wants help drafting Power Query steps and understanding an inherited query. Which documented assistant works inside Dataflow Gen2 authoring?

options.text: Copilot for Data Factory, integrated into the Dataflow Gen2 authoring experience.
options.why: Correct. Copilot is documented inside the Gen2 authoring experience for drafting and explaining queries.

options.text: The Fabric capacity metrics app.
options.why: That observes consumption; it does not author queries.

options.text: The SQL analytics endpoint.
options.why: A query surface, not an assistant.

options.text: Git integration.
options.why: Source control, not authoring assistance.

explanation: Copilot for Data Factory is the documented in-product assistant for Gen2 authoring.

title: When the notebook wins
prompt: Which requirement in the documented decision guide pushes the choice toward a Spark notebook over a dataflow?

options.text: The transformation needs custom code — e.g., a model call or stateful logic Power Query cannot express.
options.why: Correct. The guide routes custom-code transformations to notebooks.

options.text: The team prefers visual step-by-step authoring.
options.why: That is the dataflow's strength, not the notebook's.

options.text: The data is small and the logic is a simple filter.
options.why: That is Copy-activity territory in the guide.

options.text: The destination must be a Warehouse table.
options.why: Both dataflows and notebooks can write there; destination alone does not decide.

explanation: The decision guide's axis is what the transformation needs: managed Power Query (dataflow) versus custom code (notebook) versus movement (copy).

title: End-to-end tutorial shape
prompt: The end-to-end Dataflow Gen2 tutorial demonstrates a full solution shape. Which sequence matches its documented flow?

options.text: Ingest and transform with a dataflow into a destination, then orchestrate/schedule it, with monitoring through refresh history.
options.why: Correct. The tutorial walks authoring → destination → scheduling/monitoring as one solution shape.

options.text: Author a semantic model, then attach a dataflow to its partitions.
options.why: That inverts the Gen2 architecture; destinations are the storage layer.

options.text: Mirror every source, then query with KQL.
options.why: Mirroring is a different feature family entirely.

options.text: Author a Real-Time dashboard from the dataflow editor.
options.why: Not part of the dataflow tutorial's flow.

explanation: The end-to-end tutorial's arc is author → land → orchestrate/monitor, which is the Gen2 solution shape.

title: KQL as a destination
prompt: Real-Time Intelligence consumers want the cleaned entities streamed into a KQL database. Which data destination serves that in Dataflow Gen2?

options.text: The Azure Data Explorer / KQL database destination.
options.why: Correct. A KQL (Azure Data Explorer) destination is among the documented data outputs.

options.text: There is no KQL destination; only an eventstream can fill an Eventhouse.
options.why: The documented destination list includes KQL databases.

options.text: The Warehouse destination, queried with KQL.
options.why: Warehouses are queried with T-SQL, not KQL.

options.text: The OneLake file destination, parsed by KQL.
options.why: KQL databases ingest managed tables; the destination exists directly.

explanation: KQL databases are a documented Gen2 destination, so analytics-ready entities can feed RTI consumers without an intermediate eventstream.

title: Gateway and destination pairing
prompt: A dataflow ingests from an on-premises SQL Server (via gateway) and lands in a Fabric lakehouse. Where does each connection apply?

options.text: The gateway applies to the source connection; the lakehouse destination is a Fabric-internal connection that does not need the gateway.
options.why: Correct. Gateways bridge cloud-to-on-prem for sources; Fabric destinations are cloud-internal.

options.text: Both source and destination need the gateway.
options.why: The destination lives inside Fabric; there is nothing on-prem to reach.

options.text: Neither — Fabric tunnels directly into the corporate network.
options.why: No such tunneling exists; that is why gateways are required for on-prem sources.

options.text: The gateway applies to the destination only.
options.why: The on-prem side is the source.

explanation: Gateway placement follows network topology: on-prem sources need it; Fabric-internal destinations do not.

title: Schedule and parameters
prompt: A regional rollout means the same dataflow must run against different source server names per environment. Which documented mechanism parameterizes this?

options.text: Dataflow parameters, referenced in the queries and set per deployment stage/environment.
options.why: Correct. Parameters are the documented way to vary connections and values; the API even exposes dataflow parameter discovery.

options.text: Editing the M code by hand in every stage.
options.why: Fragile and exactly what parameters exist to avoid.

options.text: One dataflow per region with no parameters.
options.why: Duplication multiplies maintenance; parameters are the documented answer.

options.text: Environment variables in a .env file.
options.why: That is not a Fabric dataflow mechanism.

explanation: Parameters parameterize connections and values in the query definition, and are set per stage — the documented path for environment-specific runs.

title: What changes conceptually
prompt: A Gen1 dataflow stored its data only for models that loaded it. Moving to Gen2, what is the conceptual change a reviewer should check for?

options.text: Gen2 queries declare explicit data destinations, so the review must decide where each entity lands (and whether staging stays on).
options.why: Correct. The destination decision is new in Gen2 and is the core review point of a migration.

options.text: Gen2 removes the ability to use Power Query transformations.
options.why: Gen2 is the Power Query experience in Fabric.

options.text: Gen2 requires rewriting queries into Spark.
options.why: No rewrite is required; the M engine comes along.

options.text: Gen2 drops scheduled refresh.
options.why: Scheduled refresh remains, documented in monitoring.

explanation: The Gen1→Gen2 conceptual shift is exactly this: from model-coupled output to explicit destinations (plus staging choices) per query.

title: Scoring inside the flow
prompt: A deployed ML model endpoint should score rows as part of the dataflow's transformation. What does the documented Gen2 feature provide?

options.text: A transformation for applying ML model endpoints to query columns inside the dataflow.
options.why: Correct. Gen2 documents applying ML model endpoints as a transformation on data.

options.text: Nothing — ML scoring must always be a separate notebook run.
options.why: The documented ML-endpoints transformation exists.

options.text: A KQL function that calls the endpoint at query time.
options.why: That is a different feature family, not the dataflow transformation.

options.text: A warehouse stored procedure wrapper.
options.why: Not the documented dataflow mechanism.

explanation: Gen2 documents invoking ML model endpoints as a transformation, bringing scoring into the managed flow.

title: Three sources, one landing
prompt: Three systems must land in the same lakehouse tables: a REST API ( paginated JSON), a partner SFTP folder of CSVs, and a SQL view. Which tool assignment follows the documented decision guide?

options.text: Dataflow(s) for all three when each needs Power Query shaping before landing; Copy activities where it is pure movement.
options.why: Correct. The guide picks per-source by transformation need: shaping → dataflow, pure movement → Copy.

options.text: Three notebooks, because heterogeneous sources require code.
options.why: Heterogeneity alone does not demand code; connectors cover these shapes.

options.text: One eventstream consuming all three.
options.why: Eventstreams serve streaming ingest, not batch landing from SFTP and SQL.

options.text: Mirroring for all three.
options.why: Mirroring applies to its supported replication sources, not SFTP/REST batch landing.

explanation: The decision guide is applied per workload: transformation need selects the dataflow; pure movement selects Copy; custom code selects notebooks.

title: The rerun policy
prompt: A nightly dataflow refresh occasionally fails on a flaky source. Rather than manual reruns, what documented orchestration behavior helps?

options.text: Wrap the dataflow in a pipeline activity with an activity-level retry policy, so transient source failures rerun automatically.
options.why: Correct. Pipeline activities carry retry policies — the documented way to absorb transient failures.

options.text: Refresh twice a day and hope.
options.why: More schedules do not absorb transient failures deterministically.

options.text: Disable the refresh until the source stabilizes.
options.why: That trades data freshness for silence — not an operations answer.

options.text: Split the dataflow into ten smaller dataflows.
options.why: Fragmentation does not address transient failures.

explanation: The Dataflow activity plus retry policy is the documented pattern for transient source failures: same logic, automatic reruns.

title: Gen1 consumers keep working
prompt: A report currently reads a Gen1 dataflow's output. After a parallel Gen2 dataflow is built with its own destinations, what must change for the report to read the freshest Gen2 output?

options.text: The report's source should point at the Gen2 output (e.g., the lakehouse/warehouse tables the destinations populate), since Gen2 lands data in destinations rather than only exposing dataflow datasets.
options.why: Correct. Gen2's output lives in the destinations; consumers point there.

options.text: Nothing — Gen2 automatically retargets existing reports.
options.why: Reports keep their bindings; repointing is part of the migration.

options.text: The report must be rebuilt in DirectQuery mode.
options.why: Storage mode is unrelated to which tables feed the model.

options.text: Gen2 output can only be consumed by pipelines.
options.why: Destinations are ordinary storage consumers read from.

explanation: Consumers follow the data: Gen2 stores in declared destinations, so downstream items repoint to those tables.

title: Building the first one
prompt: Which sequence reflects the documented first-dataflow experience in Fabric?

options.text: Create the Dataflow Gen2 item, add data source queries, transform in Power Query, attach data destination(s), then save and refresh.
options.why: Correct. That is the documented authoring arc for a first dataflow.

options.text: Write M code in a warehouse, then run it as a stored procedure.
options.why: Warehouse procedures are a different engine.

options.text: Create a semantic model first, then add the dataflow inside it.
options.why: Dataflows are standalone items that models consume, not the reverse.

options.text: Start a pipeline, author the dataflow inside the Copy activity.
options.why: The Dataflow activity invokes existing dataflows; authoring happens in the item.

explanation: The documented first-run arc: item → queries → transformations → destinations → save/refresh.

title: Staging off for the big landing
prompt: A 400-million-row pass-through copy from one lakehouse table to another lands fastest with staging disabled. What is the documented trade-off when staging is off?

options.text: The query writes directly to the destination and cannot serve other queries as a stored intermediate.
options.why: Correct. Without staging there is no stored intermediate — other queries recompute the source chain themselves.

options.text: The destination table loses schema information.
options.why: Schemas derive from the query output regardless of staging.

options.text: Scheduled refresh becomes unavailable for the dataflow.
options.why: Refresh scheduling is unaffected.

options.text: The dataflow must switch to DirectQuery.
options.why: DirectQuery is a semantic-model storage mode, not a dataflow toggle.

explanation: Staging's benefit is the stored intermediate; disabling it trades that reuse for a direct, cheaper landing.

title: Naming the item
prompt: Where does a Dataflow Gen2 item live in a Fabric workspace, and what is it independent of?

options.text: It is a first-class workspace item, independent of any semantic model or notebook.
options.why: Correct. Gen2 is its own item type in the workspace.

options.text: It lives inside a semantic model as a partition.
options.why: That was the Gen1-era coupling; Gen2 items are standalone.

options.text: It lives inside a lakehouse as a hidden artifact.
options.why: It is visible at workspace level, not buried in a lakehouse.

options.text: It lives inside a pipeline as an activity definition.
options.why: Pipelines invoke dataflows; they do not contain them.

explanation: First-class item, independent lifetime, own refresh — that is the Gen2 positioning.

title: Five-minute fresh vs nightly
prompt: A dashboard needs near-real-time feed updates (seconds-fresh), separate from a nightly curated landing. Which assignment follows the documented engine guidance?

options.text: An eventstream for the streaming feed; a dataflow or copy for the nightly curated landing.
options.why: Correct. Streaming latency is eventstream territory; scheduled shaping lands with dataflows/copy.

options.text: A dataflow refreshing every five minutes for the feed.
options.why: Scheduled refresh is batch; five-minute refreshes are neither cheap nor seconds-fresh.

options.text: A notebook scheduled every five minutes for the feed.
options.why: Same batch problem, plus code ownership.

options.text: Mirroring for the dashboard feed.
options.why: Mirroring replicates supported databases, not arbitrary fast feeds.

explanation: Freshness requirement picks the engine: continuous streams to eventstream, scheduled shaping to dataflows/copy.

title: Reviewing the Save-as result
prompt: After Save-as creates the Gen2 version, which review item is new compared to the Gen1 original?

options.text: Choosing and validating data destinations (and staging) for each query.
options.why: Correct. Destinations/staging did not exist in Gen1 and are the review surface Gen2 adds.

options.text: Re-authoring every transformation in KQL.
options.why: The M queries carry over; no KQL rewrite exists.

options.text: Re-creating the model's measures.
options.why: Measures belong to models, not dataflows.

options.text: Choosing a new Semantic-model storage mode.
options.why: Storage modes belong to models, not dataflows.

explanation: The migration review centers on the new Gen2 concepts: destinations per query and the staging choices.

title: Stage-specific connections
prompt: Dev, test and production workspaces each have their own source systems. When the dataflow deploys through a deployment pipeline, what must the release process handle?

options.text: Stage-specific connection (and parameter) settings — the definition deploys, while connections/parameters are adjusted per stage per the documented CI/CD guidance.
options.why: Correct. The CI/CD page documents exactly this: definitions move, connections and parameters are configured per stage.

options.text: Nothing — connections deploy unchanged and point at the dev source from production.
options.why: That is the failure mode the per-stage settings exist to prevent.

options.text: A full re-authoring of the queries in each stage.
options.why: The definition travels; only the environment-specific settings differ.

options.text: Disabling Git integration for dataflows in production.
options.why: Source control and stage deployment are documented to work together.

explanation: Dataflow Gen2 CI/CD separates the definition (which deploys) from stage-specific connections and parameters (which the release configures) — the documented per-stage story.

title: Dataflow inside the pattern
prompt: The documented pipeline tutorial wires a dataflow into a broader run. Which ordering is sound?

options.text: Notebook prepares the source → Dataflow activity refreshes the shaped entities → downstream activities consume the landed tables.
options.why: Correct. The tutorial's shape places the Dataflow activity between preparation and consumption, with dependencies ordering the run.

options.text: Dataflow first, then the notebook that creates its source.
options.why: Dependencies run sources before consumers; this ordering fails.

options.text: Copy activity after the dataflow to move the same data again.
options.why: The dataflow already landed its output; a second copy is redundant.

options.text: The Dataflow activity cannot participate in a pipeline at all.
options.why: It is a documented activity type.

explanation: Pipeline dependencies order preparation → dataflow refresh → consumption; the tutorial demonstrates exactly that wiring.

title: Who maintains what
prompt: A governance review asks who can author and refresh dataflows. Which statement matches the documented item model?

options.text: Dataflows are workspace items governed by workspace roles and item permissions, refreshed by their owners or via pipelines with the runner's/service identity.
options.why: Correct. Standard Fabric permission semantics apply to dataflow items.

options.text: Only capacity admins can author dataflows.
options.why: Authoring follows workspace permissions, not capacity-admin exclusivity.

options.text: Dataflows inherit permissions from the semantic models that read them.
options.why: Permission flows from the item, not from its consumers.

options.text: Dataflows are tenant-global and shared by default.
options.why: They live in workspaces like other items.

explanation: Dataflows follow the standard workspace/item permission model — no special identity rules beyond documented refresh behavior.

title: The wide merge
prompt: A dataflow merges a 200-million-row source with a small lookup on a non-folded custom match. Refresh time is dominated by this step. Which documented lever helps most?

options.text: Restructure so the merge folds to the source (or staging the large side first), avoiding a full local evaluation of the big table.
options.why: Correct. The documented performance levers are folding and staging — landing the big side lets the join compute against stored data.

options.text: Increase the Power BI visual count.
options.why: Visuals are irrelevant to refresh cost.

options.text: Rename the queries to shorter names.
options.why: Naming has no performance effect.

options.text: Add more destinations to distribute the work.
options.why: More destinations add work; they do not speed the merge.

explanation: Two documented levers dominate dataflow performance: fold what the source can do, and stage large intermediates so later steps compute over stored data.

title: The empty result trap
prompt: A query returns rows in the editor preview but the destination table is empty after refresh. Which review step is most defensible first?

options.text: Compare the refresh run in monitoring (per-query outcomes) and the destination load settings (e.g., replace vs append semantics) before touching the query logic.
options.why: Correct. Monitoring plus destination configuration explains 'preview works, table empty' most directly.

options.text: Rewrite the query in SQL.
options.why: The symptom points at run/destination configuration, not language.

options.text: Delete and recreate the dataflow.
options.why: Destructive first steps are not a diagnostic.

options.text: Increase the preview row count in the editor.
options.why: Preview settings do not affect refresh outcomes.

explanation: Monitoring gives the run truth; destination load settings give the write truth. Both precede any query rewrite.

title: Templates for the estate
prompt: Fifty Gen1 dataflows exist across workspaces. Which documented aid best scales the migration beyond one-by-one save-as?

options.text: The export-template feature for moving dataflow definitions, applied per flow with the documented Gen1→Gen2 guidance for differences.
options.why: Correct. Template export is the documented scaling aid, alongside the migration guidance page.

options.text: A single tenant-wide toggle that converts everything overnight.
options.why: No such toggle is documented.

options.text: Rebuilding all flows by hand from screenshots.
options.why: The documented aids exist precisely to avoid that.

options.text: Copying the Gen1 items into the same workspace and renaming them Gen2.
options.why: Renaming does not change the generation.

explanation: Template export plus the migration guidance is the documented path when Save-as alone does not scale across an estate.

title: Gen2 vocabulary check
prompt: Which pairing of term and meaning is correct for Dataflow Gen2?

options.text: Data destination — where a query's output lands (lakehouse, warehouse, Azure SQL, KQL database, and more).
options.why: Correct. That is exactly what the term names in the documented destination experience.

options.text: Staging — a Git branch for dataflow definitions.
options.why: Staging is a data concept, not a source-control one.

options.text: Linked entities — Power BI visuals bound to the dataflow.
options.why: Linked entities relate dataflows to each other's entities, not to visuals.

options.text: Fast Copy — the monitoring view's name.
options.why: Fast Copy is a compute/copy optimization concept, not a monitoring view.

explanation: The Gen2 vocabulary: data destinations (where output lands), staging (stored intermediates), plus compute/copy optimizations — each named precisely in the documentation.

title: Append or replace
prompt: A lakehouse destination table must accumulate daily rows rather than being rebuilt each refresh. Which destination behavior should be configured, and what must the query avoid?

options.text: An append-style load for the destination, and the query must not re-emit the whole history (only the new rows) — otherwise rows duplicate.
options.why: Correct. Append semantics plus a query scoped to new data is the coherent pairing; emitting full history into append duplicates.

options.text: A replace-style load, keeping the full-history query.
options.why: Replace matches the full-history query — the opposite of the accumulate requirement.

options.text: Append with the full-history query, accepting duplicates as history.
options.why: Duplicates are not history; they are corruption of the grain.

options.text: No configuration — destinations always append.
options.why: Load behavior is a configured choice.

explanation: Load semantics and query scope must agree: append needs new-rows-only queries; replace needs full re-emit. Mismatching them is the classic duplication bug.
